questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.13
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following data path of a simple non-pipelined CPU. The registers $A, B$, $A_{1},A_{2}, \textsf{MDR},$ the $\textsf{bus}$ and the $\textsf{ALU}$ are $8$-$bit$ wide. $\textsf{SP}$ and $\textsf{MAR}$ are $16$-$bit$ registers. The $\textsf{MUX}$ is of size $8 \times (2:1)$ and the $\textsf{DEMUX}$ is of size $8 \times (1:2)$. Each memory operation takes $2$ $\textsf{CPU}$ clock cycles and uses $\textsf{MAR}$ (Memory Address Register) and $\textsf{MDR}$ (Memory Date Register). $\textsf{SP}$ can be decremented locally.

The $\textsf{CPU}$ instruction "push r" where, $r =$ $A$ or $B$ has the specification

  • $M[SP] ← r $
  • $SP ← SP - 1$

How many $\textsf{CPU}$ clock cycles are required to execute the "push r" instruction?

  1. $2$
  2. $3$
  3. $4$
  4. $5$

review.independentCheck: Two 8-bit bus transfers for 16-bit SP->MAR, one for 8-bit r->MDR, and 2-cycle memory write; local SP decrement overlaps; total 5 cycles, Option D.
review.notes: Two 8-bit bus transfers for 16-bit SP->MAR, one for 8-bit r->MDR, and 2-cycle memory write; local SP decrement overlaps; total 5 cycles, Option D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.14
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Consider an undirected, unweighted graph $G$. Let a breadth-first traversal of $G$ be done starting from a node $r$. Let $d(r,u)$ and $d(r,v)$ be the lengths of the shortest paths from $r$ to $u$ and $v$ respectively in $G$. If $u$ is visited before $v$ during the breadth-first traversal, which of the following statements is correct?

  1. $d(r,u) < d(r,v)$
  2. $d(r,u) > d(r,v)$
  3. $d(r,u) \leq d(r,v)$
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: BFS visits vertices in non-decreasing layer order; visiting u before v implies d(r,u) <= d(r,v), Option C.
review.notes: BFS visits vertices in non-decreasing layer order; visiting u before v implies d(r,u) <= d(r,v), Option C.

What is the minimum number of stacks of size $n$ required to implement a queue of size $n$?

  2. Two

review.independentCheck: Two stacks of capacity n (input and output stack) are necessary and sufficient to reverse LIFO into FIFO, Option B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.17 | UGCNET-AUG2016-III: 21
questions.subject: Programming in C
questions.questionHtml:
What is printed by the print statements in the program $P1$ assuming call by reference parameter passing?

Program P1
{
    x = 10;
    y = 3;
    func1(y,x,x);
    print x;
    print y;
}

func1(x,y,z)
{
    y = y + 4;
    z = x + y + z
}
  1. $\text{10, 3}$
  2. $\text{31, 3}$
  3. $\text{27, 7}$
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: Call-by-reference with aliased formal parameters y and z bound to P1.x yields 14 after increment and 3+14+14=31 after sum; P1.y remains 3; prints 31, 3, Option B.
review.notes: Call-by-reference with aliased formal parameters y and z bound to P1.x yields 14 after increment and 3+14+14=31 after sum; P1.y remains 3; prints 31, 3, Option B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.18
questions.subject: Programming in C
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following three C functions:

$[P1]$ 

int *g(void)
{
    int x = 10;
    return (&x);
}

$[P2]$ 

int *g(void)
{
    int *px;
    *px = 10;
    return px;
}

$[P3]$ 

int *g(void)
{
    int *px;
    px = (int*) malloc (sizeof(int));
    *px = 10;
    return px;
}

Which of the above three functions are likely to cause problems with pointers?

  1. Only $P3$
  2. Only $P1$ and $P3$
  3. Only $P1$ and $P2$
  4. $P1, P2$ and $P3$

review.independentCheck: P1 returns dangling stack pointer, P2 dereferences uninitialized wild pointer, while P3 returns valid heap allocation; only P1 and P2 cause problems, Option C.
review.notes: P1 returns dangling stack pointer, P2 dereferences uninitialized wild pointer, while P3 returns valid heap allocation; only P1 and P2 cause problems, Option C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 2.19
questions.subject: Other / Optional
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following program

Program P2
    var n : int;
    
    procedure W(var x : int)
    begin
        x = x + 1;
        print x;
    end

    procedure D
    begin
        var n : int;
        n = 3;
        W(n);
    end

    begin    \\begin P2
        n=10;
        D;
    end

If the language has dynamic scooping and parameters are passed by reference, what will be printed by the program?

  1. 10
  2. 11
  3. 3
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: Dynamic scoping resolves formal parameter x bound by reference to D.n; x is incremented from 3 to 4 and printed; output is 4, absent from A/B/C, so Option D.
review.notes: Dynamic scoping resolves formal parameter x bound by reference to D.n; x is incremented from 3 to 4 and printed; output is 4, absent from A/B/C, so Option D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2001 | Question: 15
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a weighted undirected graph with vertex set $V = \{n1, n2, n3, n4, n5, n6 \}$ and edge set $E = \{(n1,n2,2), (n1,n3,8), (n1,n6,3), (n2,n4,4), (n2,n5,12), (n3,n4,7), (n4,n5,9), (n4,n6,4)\}$.

The third value in each tuple represents the weight of the edge specified in the tuple.

  1. List the edges of a minimum spanning tree of the graph.
  2. How many distinct minimum spanning trees does this graph have?
  3. Is the minimum among the edge weights of a minimum spanning tree unique over all possible minimum spanning trees of a graph?
  4. Is the maximum among the edge weights of a minimum spanning tree unique over all possible minimum spanning tree of a graph?

review.independentCheck: Kruskal algorithm on 6 vertices selects {2, 3, 4, 7, 9} with tie at weight 4 giving exactly 2 distinct MSTs (Part B); edge weights are {2, 3, 4, 7, 9} with min 2 and max 9 invariant across all MSTs; Option B.
review.notes: Kruskal algorithm on 6 vertices selects {2, 3, 4, 7, 9} with tie at weight 4 giving exactly 2 distinct MSTs (Part B); edge weights are {2, 3, 4, 7, 9} with min 2 and max 9 invariant across all MSTs; Option B.
